skills.name: Reviewing parts of speech and spelling rules

note.text: A word’s class depends on its use: record can name a document or function as a verb. Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs can modify actions or other expressions, but endings alone do not identify every class. Inflectional spelling also depends on the base: write gives writing, plan gives planned, and study gives studied. A final -e, a consonant before y and a short stressed vowel can matter in different rules. There are exceptions and different patterns: use the relevant model rather than applying a doubling rule to all verbs.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to classify a word by its use and apply a supported inflectional spelling pattern. Builds on: Form Four word classes and computed verb forms. Leads to: study explanations, tense revision and sentence structure.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original models: The careful member reviews a clear record. Members record their decision carefully. Compare {ing("write")}, {past("plan")} and {past("study")}. Careful describes a member; carefully describes the manner of reviewing or recording in an appropriate sentence. The grammatical role and the spelling operation need separate explanations.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Read the whole phrase, identify what the word contributes, then state the spelling change required. Check the base and suffix. Do not assume that every word ending in -ly must be an adverb or that every -ed form doubles a consonant.
